The intraoral examination revealed diffuse ragged grayish-white plaques bilaterally on the buccal and labial mucosa (Figures 1-4). The patient was aware of the lesions and reported biting them frequently.

in_text_mentions: A biopsy of the left premolar-molar buccal mucosa was submitted for microscopical evaluation and revealed parakeratosis, acanthosis, and spongiosis at the epithelial surface (Figure 5). Extensive vacuolation of suprabasal keratinocytes was observed, as well as dyskeratotic cells exhibiting dense perinuclear eosinophilic condensation (Figures 6-7). There was no evidence of dysplasia or candidal hyphae.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient clinical photograph of the oral cavity showing white-to-light-rose, fissured spongy plaques on the buccal mucosa and ventral tongue, the textbook presentation of oral white sponge nevus, explicitly attributed to oral WSN in the caption of a disease-focused article (novel keratin 13 variant family with WSN). B: Real patient clinical photograph showing thick white fissured epithelium lining the inner labia minora, i.e., genital white sponge nevus, explicitly stated in the caption; the article notes none of the examined males had genital WSN, consistent with a female family member. C: Real patient clinical photograph showing thick white epithelium of the labia extending over the introitus, i.e., genital white sponge nevus, explicitly stated in the caption; introitus involvement is visible but not covered by the provided vocabulary, so it is proposed as a new finding.

Histologic findings are characteristic of white sponge nevus, including acanthosis, hyperparakeratosis, and keratinocyte vacuolization with characteristic perinuclear eosinophilic condensation, which is not necessarily pathognomonic [9, 10].
